heuristics.rule: Subtract equity entirely and assess whether remaining compensation meets living expenses before accepting a startup offer.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a startup offer with significant equity as part of the compensation pitch...
heuristics.action: ...remove equity from the calculation entirely and evaluate whether base salary alone covers your financial needs
heuristics.because: ~90% of startups fail, dilution can reduce a 1% stake to 0.3%, liquidation preferences reduce payouts by 60–80%, and options often cost 20–50% of annual salary to exercise — making equity unreliable as income

heuristics.rule: Evaluate a role by three questions — what will you own, what decisions will you make, and who will you influence — not by title.
heuristics.condition: When comparing offers with different titles or trying to assess the real scope of a role...
heuristics.action: ...replace title comparison with a structured assessment of decision surface, autonomy, and organizational reach
heuristics.because: Startups inflate titles because they can't compete on comp, and Big Tech has so many leveling bands that 'Senior' means wildly different things across orgs — title is a noisy signal

heuristics.rule: Optimize for your next two jobs, not your entire career or just this year's salary.
heuristics.condition: When making a startup vs. Big Tech decision at any career stage...
heuristics.action: ...evaluate how this role positions you for the role after the next one, not just immediate compensation or prestige
heuristics.because: Neither path is wrong if you commit fully, but the sequencing and downstream optionality matter more than any single job's immediate rewards

heuristics.rule: If you want both startup and Big Tech experience, do Big Tech first.
heuristics.condition: When early in your career and uncertain about sequencing startup vs. Big Tech...
heuristics.action: ...start at Big Tech to preserve optionality in both directions
heuristics.because: Big Tech → startup is easy and always available; startup → Big Tech requires either startup success or strong prior credentials, meaning starting at a startup narrows Big Tech entry options

heuristics.rule: Early career (0–5 years): prioritize learning velocity over everything else, including compensation.
heuristics.condition: When evaluating offers in the first five years of a PM career...
heuristics.action: ...weight learning speed and breadth of exposure above salary, title, or brand name
heuristics.because: Startup experience at a failed company with meaningful scope still teaches more than 2 years as a mid-level PM in a large Big Tech team — the compound returns on early learning outweigh short-term comp differences

heuristics.rule: Set a 1-week information-gathering deadline, then decide and commit.
heuristics.condition: When stuck in prolonged deliberation between startup and Big Tech offers...
heuristics.action: ...time-box due diligence to one week, then make a full commitment
heuristics.because: Half-hearted commitment produces poor outcomes in either environment — the quality of execution after the decision matters more than marginal improvement in the decision itself

heuristics.rule: Match risk tolerance to life stage, not to abstract career ambition.
heuristics.condition: When assessing whether startup risk is appropriate for your situation...
heuristics.action: ...inventory your financial obligations (mortgage, dependents) before treating startup equity as a viable wealth-building strategy
heuristics.because: Startup runway failure with a mortgage and family creates real financial exposure — rational risk calibration means taking more risk when you can absorb downside, not when you most want upside

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Risk tolerance changes completely based on whether you have a mortgage, dependents, or other fixed obligations — the same startup offer is a rational bet at 25 and a dangerous one at 38 with kids
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Inventory fixed monthly obligations (mortgage/rent, dependents, debt service) and calculate whether base salary alone at the startup covers them without equity

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A startup's burn rate and runway determine whether your equity has any time to vest and whether you'll still have a job in 18 months
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask directly for MRR, customer churn rates, current burn rate, runway until next funding round, path to profitability, and contingency plans if funding fails — treat inability to answer specifically as a red flag

decision_factors.factor: Equity structure details (liquidation preferences, exercise window)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Two offers with identical equity percentages can have radically different actual payouts depending on liquidation preference stacking and exercise window length
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask for the cap table summary, liquidation preference terms on all existing rounds, and exercise window length (90 days vs. 5-year extended windows are materially different)

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Actual scope of ownership determines learning velocity, resume credibility, and career trajectory more than title or compensation
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: What will I own? What decisions will I make unilaterally vs. need approval for? Who will I influence organizationally? Compare answers across offers directly

decision_factors.factor: Career stage and desired trajectory (5-year vision)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The right choice depends entirely on where you want to be in 5 years — specific skills needed, network required, and financial position targeted
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Define the 5-year target with specificity (not 'senior leader' but specific skills, network type, and financial position), then evaluate which path creates more of those prerequisites

decision_factors.factor: Manager quality and team shipping record
decision_factors.why_it_matters: At Big Tech, manager quality and recent team output predict your actual learning and promotion trajectory more than org brand
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask what the team shipped in the last 12 months (ask for 3 specific products), how the manager makes decisions, promotion time-to-promo at your level in this specific org, and why the role exists

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Startup success opens all doors; startup failure opens startup doors but not Big Tech; Big Tech opens most doors but can pigeonhole — sequencing affects which doors stay open
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Map the likely resume outcomes (success, failure, middling) for each path and assess which downstream options matter most to you

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Startup provides breadth and speed under uncertainty; Big Tech provides depth and formal training — the right choice depends on which gap you need to fill
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Audit your current skill gaps: if you lack breadth and exposure to ambiguity, startup accelerates; if you lack structured frameworks and scale exposure, Big Tech accelerates

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a startup offer with compelling equity
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Options may cost 20–50% of your annual salary to exercise within 90 days of leaving — meaning you can't afford to leave even if the role stops being right for you, creating a golden handcuff made of paper
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career PMs who join at a meaningful strike price and then find the company stagnating but can't afford to exercise and walk away

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a startup early in your career for the breadth experience
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the startup fails, Big Tech entry becomes harder — you need either a Big Tech credential already or a successful startup exit to be competitive for Big Tech roles later
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Early-career PMs who go startup-first without Big Tech credentials and then want to transition to Big Tech after a failed startup

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying at Big Tech for the structured growth and predictable compensation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Learning plateaus are real by mid-career (5–10 years), and individual contribution impact gets lost in the machine — you can have a strong career on paper while your actual skill development stagnates
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Mid-career PMs who have strong reviews and good comp but haven't been forced to operate under real ambiguity or resource constraints

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Taking a startup Director or VP title
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The title is compensation substitution, not scope recognition — Big Tech will re-level you to your actual scope when you try to make the transition, and the inflated title may actually raise red flags
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who optimize for title at startups and then discover Big Tech recruiter leveling ignores startup titles entirely

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Delaying a Big Tech → startup move until late career (10+ years)
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The transition becomes harder, not easier — Big Tech credentialism matters more for senior hires, and startup ecosystems become less accessible the longer you stay in large-org operating models
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Senior Big Tech PMs who assume they can 'always go to a startup later' without realizing the window narrows

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Treating startup equity as compensation that offsets lower base salary
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Even if the company succeeds, dilution through multiple funding rounds can reduce a 1% stake to 0.3%, and liquidation preferences mean investors get paid first — reducing actual payout by 60–80% relative to headline valuation
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PMs who accept below-living-expense base salaries on the assumption that equity will compensate, especially those with financial obligations

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a startup offer where base salary doesn't cover living expenses, betting on equity to make up the difference
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Founders pitch the equity upside compellingly and candidates anchor on the 0.5–2% number without modeling dilution, liquidation preferences, or failure probability
failure_patterns.consequence: Financial stress within 12–18 months as the equity thesis fails to materialize, often forcing a hasty exit under duress rather than on your own terms
warning_signs: Base salary is more than 30% below market for your level and location
You find yourself calculating what 1% of the projected exit valuation would be worth before asking about current MRR

failure_patterns.pattern: Optimizing for title at a startup instead of scope and decision authority
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Title is visible and legible; decision authority is abstract and harder to evaluate during interviews — candidates default to the visible signal
failure_patterns.consequence: A Director title with no real decision surface produces a weak resume story and re-leveling surprises when transitioning to Big Tech
warning_signs: You're excited about the title before you've understood what you'll actually own
The recruiter led with title early in the conversation without probing your scope expectations

failure_patterns.pattern: Joining a startup without conducting financial due diligence on runway and burn rate
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Candidates feel it's inappropriate or aggressive to ask financial questions, and founders who 'talk more about vision than customers' successfully redirect the conversation
failure_patterns.consequence: Joining a company with 6 months of runway and no clear path to next funding, resulting in layoff before meaningful equity vests
warning_signs: Founder gives inspiring vision answers but pivots away from specific MRR or runway questions
You leave the final round without knowing the current burn rate or months of runway remaining

failure_patterns.pattern: Making the startup vs. Big Tech decision without defining a 5-year vision first
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The decision feels urgent (offer deadline) and both paths have real appeal — candidates decide reactively based on whichever pitch was more recent or emotionally compelling
failure_patterns.consequence: Half-hearted commitment to whichever path is chosen, producing poor outcomes because neither environment rewards ambivalence
warning_signs: You're evaluating the offers against each other rather than against a defined personal target state
Your decision rationale changes depending on who you talked to most recently

failure_patterns.pattern: Starting a career at a startup without Big Tech credentials and then finding Big Tech entry blocked after startup failure
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Early-career PMs underestimate the asymmetry of the path — they assume startup experience is universally valued, not understanding that Big Tech values either startup success or prior Big Tech credentials
failure_patterns.consequence: Trapped in the startup ecosystem without the option to transition to Big Tech for stability or credentialism unless they go back to school or find a breakout success
warning_signs: You're planning a startup-first career path without a contingency for what happens if the startup fails within 2 years
You assume that meaningful scope at a failed startup translates directly to Big Tech interview success

diagnostic_questions.question: If you subtract equity entirely, does the base salary cover your monthly fixed obligations?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you are gambling with money you need versus money you can afford to lose — this is the foundational risk calibration question
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Then equity is upside — proceed to evaluate the equity structure (dilution, liquidation preferences, exercise window) as a bonus, not as compensation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is a disqualifying condition unless you have significant savings or other income — the offer is asking you to take on financial risk you cannot absorb

diagnostic_questions.question: What are your fixed financial obligations right now — mortgage or rent, dependents, debt service?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Your actual risk tolerance capacity, which changes the entire startup vs. Big Tech calculus regardless of stated preferences
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If obligations are significant, startup base salary risk becomes a real financial exposure, not just career risk — weight Big Tech's compensation predictability much higher
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If obligations are minimal (early career, no dependents, renting), startup financial risk is manageable — learning velocity and scope become the primary decision variables

diagnostic_questions.question: What specific skills, network, and financial position do you want to have in 5 years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the person has a concrete target state or is evaluating offers in a vacuum — without this, any comparison is noise
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Map each offer's likely outcome against the 5-year target — which path creates more of the prerequisites you've identified?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The decision cannot be made well until this is defined — spend time on the 5-year vision before evaluating either offer on its merits

diagnostic_questions.question: Can the startup founder tell you the current MRR, customer churn rate, burn rate, and months of runway without hedging?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the startup has the financial transparency and stability that makes the risk calculable, and whether the founder is operating with real customer traction or primarily vision
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Proceed to evaluate liquidation preferences, exercise window length, and dilution history from prior funding rounds
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is a red flag — a founder who talks more about vision than customers or can't give specific runway numbers is either uninformed or evasive, both of which are disqualifying

diagnostic_questions.question: At the Big Tech role, what has this specific team shipped in the last 12 months — can you name three products?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the team is actually shipping or is in a planning/reorganization holding pattern — a strong brand doesn't mean this particular team is executing
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Probe the manager's decision-making style and the promotion trajectory (time-to-promo at your level in this specific org)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: High turnover or inability to name recent shipped work suggests either a reorganization in progress or a low-momentum team — probe why the role exists before proceeding

diagnostic_questions.question: Where are you in your career — 0–5 years, 5–10 years, or 10+ years of PM experience?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Which phase of the learning vs. stability vs. credentialism tradeoff you're in — the right answer genuinely differs by career stage
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If early (0–5): learning velocity dominates the decision, and meaningful startup scope may outweigh a Big Tech role with narrow initial scope
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If mid (5–10): assess whether Big Tech has produced a real learning plateau; if late (10+): Big Tech credentialism matters more for senior hires and startup transitions become harder

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the exercise window on the startup options — standard 90 days or an extended window?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether you will be able to afford to leave the company if the role stops being right for you, and the actual cost of the optionality you're accepting
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If extended (5+ years): the exit trap is much less severe — you can leave without immediately paying 20–50% of annual salary to preserve options
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If 90 days: model explicitly what it would cost you to exercise at current strike price and whether you could afford it — if not, you are accepting a golden handcuff

industry_realities.common_belief: Startup equity compensates for lower base salary — a 1% stake in a successful company makes up for years of below-market pay
industry_realities.actual_reality: ~90% of startups fail entirely; dilution through funding rounds can reduce 1% to 0.3%; liquidation preferences reduce actual payouts by 60–80%; and options often cost 20–50% of annual salary to exercise on departure — the expected value of startup equity is far lower than the headline number
industry_realities.implication: Treat equity as a lottery ticket, not compensation — evaluate the offer on base salary alone and treat equity as potential upside you might never see

industry_realities.common_belief: A Director or VP title at a startup signals seniority that transfers to Big Tech
industry_realities.actual_reality: Startups hand out senior titles because they can't compete on comp — Big Tech will re-level you to your actual decision surface and scope when evaluating your background, ignoring startup title inflation
industry_realities.implication: Evaluate startup roles by what you'll own and decide, not by the title offered — a Senior PM title with real scope beats a VP title with no decision authority for actual career development

industry_realities.common_belief: Startup experience is universally valuable and opens doors to Big Tech if you want to transition
industry_realities.actual_reality: Startup → Big Tech requires either startup success (proving yourself) or strong prior credentials (Big Tech experience or top-tier education) — startup failure with no prior Big Tech experience narrows Big Tech entry significantly
industry_realities.implication: If you want both experiences, doing Big Tech first preserves optionality in both directions — starting at a startup narrows your Big Tech entry options unless the startup succeeds

industry_realities.common_belief: Big Tech provides consistent, accelerating growth because of the resources, training, and talent density
industry_realities.actual_reality: Learning plateaus at Big Tech are real by mid-career (5–10 years) — structured training and scale exposure don't substitute for operating under real ambiguity and resource constraints, which Big Tech insulates you from
industry_realities.implication: Mid-career Big Tech PMs should actively audit whether they are still learning at rate, not assume that good reviews equal continued development

industry_realities.common_belief: 'Senior PM' means roughly the same thing across companies
industry_realities.actual_reality: Big Tech has so many leveling bands that 'Senior' means wildly different things at different orgs — the title is a noisy signal for actual scope, compensation, and career stage
industry_realities.implication: Use the three scope questions (what will you own, what decisions will you make, who will you influence) to translate across companies rather than comparing titles directly

industry_realities.common_belief: Taking startup risk is admirable at any career stage — it shows ambition and tolerance for uncertainty
industry_realities.actual_reality: Risk tolerance should evolve with life stage — taking startup risk with a mortgage and dependents is not bold, it's a mismatch between risk capacity and risk exposure; the source explicitly states 'matching risk to life stage is rational, not timid'
industry_realities.implication: Recalibrate startup risk appetite based on actual financial obligations rather than treating high risk tolerance as a fixed personality virtue

industry_realities.common_belief: Career advice about startup vs. Big Tech applies generically regardless of where you are in your career
industry_realities.actual_reality: The right choice differs materially by career stage: early career should prioritize learning velocity; mid-career should assess plateau risk; late career faces harder startup transitions and Big Tech credentialism matters more for senior hires
industry_realities.implication: Discount career advice that doesn't specify which career stage it applies to — stage-specific reasoning is the variable most generic PM career advice ignores

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Anchors on the headline equity number (e.g., '1% of the company') and calculates best-case exit scenarios to justify accepting below-market base salary
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Subtracts equity entirely from the calculation first, evaluates whether base salary meets obligations, then treats equity as probabilistic upside — models dilution, liquidation preferences, and exercise costs explicitly
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Junior framing leads to accepting financial risk you can't absorb; senior framing surfaces whether the offer is actually viable before upside speculation

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares titles across offers and anchors on brand name prestige or team size as proxies for role quality
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Ignores title and asks three specific questions: what will I own, what decisions will I make, who will I influence — uses answers to reconstruct actual scope independent of title or brand
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Title and brand are noisy signals that actively mislead — scope questions reveal what the role will actually develop in you and what you can credibly claim on a resume in 2 years

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats risk tolerance as a stable personality trait — 'I'm a risk-taker so startup is right for me' — without connecting it to current financial obligations
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats risk tolerance as a dynamic variable that should match life stage and financial exposure — explicitly inventories obligations before assessing whether startup risk is rational
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Mismatched risk capacity and risk exposure creates real financial harm, not just career risk — the framing determines whether you're making a bet you can actually afford to lose

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Deliberates indefinitely between options, changing preference based on most recent conversation, and optimizes for the current offer rather than a defined target state
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Defines a 5-year vision with specific skills, network, and financial targets first; evaluates each offer against that target; time-boxes information gathering and commits fully to whichever path aligns better
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Without a defined target state, offer evaluation is noise — and half-hearted commitment produces poor outcomes in either environment regardless of which choice was 'correct'

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Asks about culture, growth opportunities, and team dynamics — avoids financial questions as too aggressive or inappropriate
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Asks directly for MRR, churn rates, burn rate, runway, liquidation preference terms, and exercise window length — treats inability to answer specifically as a disqualifying red flag
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Financial due diligence determines whether the startup can actually deliver on the scope and learning promises — joining without it means accepting risk you haven't quantified

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Optimizes for the current offer in isolation — 'which job is better right now?' — without modeling how each choice affects downstream options
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Optimizes for the next two jobs — models how each path affects resume credibility, optionality, and trajectory, including the asymmetry that Big Tech → startup is always available but startup → Big Tech requires credentials or success
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Career paths have path dependencies — early sequencing decisions close or open options that matter significantly at mid and late career stages
